title: Will AI make your degree pointless?
description:
AI isn’t just occasionally going rogue…(Open AI and Meta we’re looking at you) it’s also changing the world of work. Nearly 70% of college students in the US said they thought AI would make it harder to find a job in a recent survey - and 22% said that they’ve changed what they’re deciding to study at university because of this. They’re not the only ones… students all over the world are thinking about how to AI-proof their future careers.

In this episode, we go to the University College London campus to speak to three students: Omer, who’s studying French and German, Zahra, who’s studying entrepreneurship, and Allie, who’s just graduated from Kings College after completing her law studies. They tell us how they think AI could change the course of their careers, how they’re adapting to the new technology, and if their degrees will still be helpful in the face of AI.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討人工智慧 AI 是否會削弱大學學位的價值，以及學生該如何因應 AI 對未來職涯的影響。主持人 Hannah Gelbart 前往倫敦大學學院訪問三位學生。主修創業學的 Zara 認為 AI 帶來了人機協作的新契機；主修語言學的 Omer 指出 AI 雖然擅長翻譯，但無法取代面對面溝通的感情連結與文化理解；畢業於法律系的 Allie 則表示法律界將 AI 視為容易出錯且產生幻覺的「初級助理」，因此仍需人類嚴格監督。儘管學生們對缺少基礎實務經驗或語言學位被誤解等風險感到擔憂，但他們一致認為大學學位在培養人際技能與生活體驗上依然不可或缺，主張結合 AI 工具與人類獨特優勢來迎接未來。
summaryEn: In this episode of the BBC podcast What in the World, host Hannah Gelbart visits University College London to talk with three students—Zara (entrepreneurship), Omer (languages), and Allie (law)—about how artificial intelligence is shaping their degrees and future careers. While acknowledging potential risks such as automated entry-level work and misconceptions about certain majors, the students remain optimistic about their prospects. They emphasize that while AI can assist with translation and routine legal research, human qualities like emotional connection, cultural context, critical supervision, and leadership are irreplaceable. Ultimately, they agree that university degrees retain immense value for personal growth and practical life experience, advising future students to pair AI tools with uniquely human strengths.
